retrieval_ledger.snippet: The ad signals an expansion of the White House's controversial use of government funds to air pieces that resemble campaign advertisements.
retrieval_ledger.page_text:
The Trump administration put out a new ad this weekend as part of its “PSA” campaign, this time showing President Donald Trump walking down a hallway as he asks people to join him in his fight to “expel the warmongers from our government.”

The ad — which at the end says it was “Paid for by the U.S. government” — is nearly identical to an ad put out by Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.

Trump posted that ad to Truth Social in January 2024. The repurposed ad now includes “Paid for by the U.S. government.” But it excludes the last few seconds of the 2024 ad, which ends with text reading “Join President Trump’s fight to save America” and his 2024 campaign logo.

The ad signals an expansion of the White House’s controversial use of government funds to air pieces that resemble campaign advertisements. Last week, the White House ran a television ad in which Trump described how he wanted to “defeat communism,” set to the song “Love Me” by JMSN. The White House has called the ads “public service announcements.”

In the latest ad, dramatic black-and-white video shows President Trump walking down a hallway with audio of him saying it is the “final battle” and vowing to “demolish the deep state” and “throw off the sick political class that hates our country.”

“We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” it concludes.

### FOR SUBSCRIBERSVoters want the Iran war to end. It’s not that easy.

### FOR SUBSCRIBERSAre we approaching a new era of Alzheimer’s prevention?

### FOR SUBSCRIBERSVoters want the Iran war to end. It’s not that easy.

### FOR SUBSCRIBERSAre we approaching a new era of Alzheimer’s prevention?

Federal law requires political advertisers to submit certain public disclosures and generally bans using public funds for political advertising. Since the administration maintains the ads are public service announcements, it’s not clear whether those disclosures are available. The White House has not released a specific source of government funding used to air the ads.

AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm, has estimated that the administration has spent more than $1.7 million to run these ads, which have been running heavily in recent days during prominent television programming like football games, Sunday morning news shows and primetime broadcast shows. That having been said, AdImpact doesn’t have full visibility into airings on every cable channel in every market in the country, hampering that estimate.

The White House defended the ad Sunday, pointing NBC News to a statement it had offered last week when it commented on the other ads released by the administration.

“These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad. The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country,” a White House spokesperson said.

Another White House official pushed back on the line of questioning: “The PSAs are clearly not political. The president is not on the ballot, and the ads don’t have a call to action.”

The White House did not specifically respond to NBC News’ question about the ad’s being nearly identical to the 2024 Trump campaign ad.

A White House spokesperson also pointed to past examples of ads released by former administrations, including an ad by George W. Bush’s Department of Health and Human Services, a social media campaign by Barack Obama’s Environmental Protection Agency in 2014 and 2015 and an effort by Joe Biden’s administration encouraging Covid-19 vaccination.

The nonpartisan Government Accountability Office dinged the Bush and Obama ad campaigns — Bush’s for not properly disclosing the government was the source and Obama’s for violating “publicity or propaganda and anti-lobbying provisions.”

White House communications director Steven Cheung defended the recent pro-Trump ads Sunday on social media, writing, “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv.”

CNN and The New York Times were first to report about the ad’s being almost identical to Trump’s 2024 campaign ad.

Spending taxpayer dollars on the ads has raised legal and ethical concerns and condemnation from both parties.

“This is the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and utterly illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars,” congressional Democratic appropriators wrote in a letter Friday addressed to White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

The letter was signed by Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash.; Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I.; Rep. Rosa De Lauro, D-Conn.; and Rep. Steny Hoyer, D-Md.

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said Sunday in an interview with CBS that public officials should not “spend public money on private ads for themselves.”

By — Julie Carr Smyth, Associated Press Julie Carr Smyth, Associated Press Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ramaswamy-campaign-says-it-produced-ad-with-amy-actons-mother-and-will-spend-millions-to-promote-it Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Ramaswamy campaign says it produced ad with Amy Acton's mother and will spend millions to promote it Politics Oct 21, 2026 2:51 PM EST COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's team confirmed late Tuesday that it produced a controversial advertisement featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, and the campaign said it will spend $4 million to promote it despite facing bipartisan rebuke for dredging up the painful childhood of his Democratic opponent in Ohio's governor's race. WATCH: Vance says he's 'disgusted' by Republicans 'whining' about Ramaswamy attack ad The decision exacerbates a deeply personal element in one of the country's most closely watched and expensive campaigns for state office. Questions about the video will likely shadow Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire who previously ran for president but has never before held public office, in the final two weeks of the contest. Democrats said he was growing desperate at a moment when more than 676,000 people have already cast ballots in Ohio. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The advertisement features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her "a liar" and insinuating she has mental health issues. Acton, Ohio's former public health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather was indicted for raping Acton. The video's origins were initially murky when it started circulating online. It first surfaced in a post by an Ohio political blogger, then spread across social media. It did not include the "paid for" tag that is legally required to air on television so viewers can know who produced and paid for it. D.J. Brynes, who blogs as "The Rooster," told CNN he got the video from a voter who viewed it as part of a poll and recorded it. READ MORE: Trump wants the midterms to be all about him. Based on Democrats' ads, they are happy to oblige Connie Luck, a spokesperson for Ramaswamy's campaign, said Acton's mother was not paid for the one-minute video, which she said will stream online and air on television. Acton spent Tuesday condemning Ramaswamy for the ad even before his campaign confirmed its provenance. "I won't normalize somebody who has said that my childhood is just something I'm complaining about, who today just released an ad using my birth mother, who I was removed from at the age of 12 for severe abuse and neglect, and sexual abuse," she told Spectrum News, a cable news outlet in Ohio. She said Ramaswamy made similar personal attacks during his run for the Republican presidential nomination two years ago, calling it "a lifelong pattern." READ MORE: After taxpayer-funded ads glorifying Trump sparked backlash, he says his super PAC will pay instead Ramaswamy's campaign initially issued a statement that did not address whether he was responsible for the ad or knew who produced it. In the earlier statement, Luck said Acton "has some serious problems with the truth that the public needs to be aware of." Democrats and Republicans condemn the ad Casey Putsch, a car designer and YouTube provocateur who competed against Ramaswamy for the Republican nomination for governor, said on social media that he would be voting for Acton in the wake of the ad's release. He called the video "pretty damn low." Acton's campaign released a statement from her brother, Philip Stearns, who said the two were removed from their mother Donna Arthur's custody as children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted for raping Acton as a child. Acton has not seen Arthur, whose last known address was in Pennsylvania, since they were in a courtroom together in 1978. WATCH: Ohio becomes midterm battleground after years of Republican wins Later Tuesday, the Acton campaign released a video featuring Stearns, who recalls his older sister taking "the worst" of the abuse they faced as children in order to protect him and disparages Ramaswamy and his allies for exploiting the situation. According to police and court documents obtained by The Associated Press, Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of his stepdaughter, then 12, in July 1978, after Acton's biological father reported him to authorities. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur pleaded not guilty. He was indicted by a grand jury that September, but failed to show at a court hearing and remained a fugitive until at least 1981. He has since died. High-profile Republicans who back Ramaswamy — including Donald Trump Jr. and influencer Laura Loomer — elevated the video in online posts. But others joined Democrats in condemning the ad. Meghan McCain called it "dastardly" and Dan Hauser, a strategist for Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, said he deleted his post sharing the video once he realized "the very serious accusations that caused their issues." The Democrat running for U.S. Senate in Ohio, Sherrod Brown, described the spot as "disgusting" and said everyone — including his opponent, Sen. Jon Husted — should be willing to condemn it. Husted's campaign didn't respond to a request for comment. Associated Press writer Ali Swenson in New York contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Senator John Cornyn's campaign has released a lengthy digital ad detailing what the campaign calls 'The Ken Paxton Scandal Timeline They Don't Want You to See.'

The six-minute long ad details a number of allegations involving the Texas Attorney General from securities fraud charges to his impeachment in the Texas House.

The ad comes just two days after the Texas primary resulted in the two facing each other in a May runoff.

After the Primary results, President Trump said he would endorse one and ask the other to drop out but Paxton initially said he would not drop out of the race.

Politico reported Thursday that President Trump may be leaning toward endorsing Senator Cornyn after Attorney General Paxton initially said he would not drop out if the president endorsed Cornyn.

We are monitoring the Paxton campaign if he releases any rebuttal ad against Cornyn.

retrieval_ledger.snippet: This site provides summary information about, and access to, the “public inspection file” contact us at 1-877-480-3201. Phone: 1-888-225-5322 1-844-432-2275 Missing:  preserved  copy  verified  transcript  Cornyn
retrieval_ledger.page_text:
## Public Inspection Files

This site provides summary information about, and access to, the “public inspection file” (or “public file”) for the following types of entities: licensed full-service radio and television broadcast stations, Class A television stations, cable television systems, direct broadcast satellite (“DBS”) providers, and satellite radio (also referred to as “Satellite Digital Audio Radio Services” or “SDARS”) licensees.

The Commission first adopted rules requiring broadcast stations to keep a public file more than 40 years ago and certain political programming files have been public for nearly 75 years. The public file for broadcast stations contains a variety of information about each station’s operations and service to its community of license, including information about political time sold or given away by each station, quarterly lists of the most significant programs each station aired concerning issues of importance to its community, data on ownership of each station and active applications each station has filed with the Commission. The Commission adopted the public inspection file requirement to "make information to which the public already has a right more readily available, so that the public will be encouraged to play a more active part in dialogue with broadcast licensees."

Cable, DBS, and SDARS entities also have public and political file requirements. These entities’ political file requirements are substantially similar to those of television and radio broadcasters. Apart from the political file, however, cable, DBS, and SDARS entities’ other public file requirements differ somewhat from the public file requirements applicable to broadcasters.

**View the complete list of the items** that must be placed in the file.

  


---

### FIND A TV / FM / AM STATION, CABLE SYSTEM, DBS PROVIDER, OR SDARS LICENSEE

For broadcast stations, you may enter a call sign (e.g., WXYZ), network affiliation (e.g., NBC), channel number (e.g., 26), or facility ID number (e.g., 123456). For CABLE systems, you may enter PSID or a ZIP code. For DBS providers or SDARS licensees, you may enter the name of the entity.

records.visible_text:
Senator John Cornyn's campaign has released a lengthy digital ad detailing what the campaign calls 'The Ken Paxton Scandal Timeline They Don't Want You to See.'

The six-minute long ad details a number of allegations involving the Texas Attorney General from securities fraud charges to his impeachment in the Texas House.

The ad comes just two days after the Texas primary resulted in the two facing each other in a May runoff.

After the Primary results, President Trump said he would endorse one and ask the other to drop out but Paxton initially said he would not drop out of the race.

Politico reported Thursday that President Trump may be leaning toward endorsing Senator Cornyn after Attorney General Paxton initially said he would not drop out if the president endorsed Cornyn.

We are monitoring the Paxton campaign if he releases any rebuttal ad against Cornyn.

S12:P1:P6.literal_quote:
Senator John Cornyn's campaign has released a lengthy digital ad detailing what the campaign calls 'The Ken Paxton Scandal Timeline They Don't Want You to See.'

The six-minute long ad details a number of allegations involving the Texas Attorney General from securities fraud charges to his impeachment in the Texas House.

The ad comes just two days after the Texas primary resulted in the two facing each other in a May runoff.

After the Primary results, President Trump said he would endorse one and ask the other to drop out but Paxton initially said he would not drop out of the race.

Politico reported Thursday that President Trump may be leaning toward endorsing Senator Cornyn after Attorney General Paxton initially said he would not drop out if the president endorsed Cornyn.

We are monitoring the Paxton campaign if he releases any rebuttal ad against Cornyn.

Senator John Cornyn's campaign has released a lengthy digital ad detailing what the campaign calls 'The Ken Paxton Scandal Timeline They Don't Want You to See.'

The six-minute long ad details a number of allegations involving the Texas Attorney General from securities fraud charges to his impeachment in the Texas House.

The ad comes just two days after the Texas primary resulted in the two facing each other in a May runoff.

After the Primary results, President Trump said he would endorse one and ask the other to drop out but Paxton initially said he would not drop out of the race.

Politico reported Thursday that President Trump may be leaning toward endorsing Senator Cornyn after Attorney General Paxton initially said he would not drop out if the president endorsed Cornyn.

We are monitoring the Paxton campaign if he releases any rebuttal ad against Cornyn.
